newsitem.title: CHINA: China premier lashes out at unfair trade practices.
newsitem.headline: China premier lashes out at unfair trade practices.

text.p: Chinese Premier Li Peng told World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero on Tuesday that Beijing's long-delayed entry to the global trade body would benefit China and the world but hit out at unfair trading practices.

"China cannot develop without the world and the world cannot develop without China," state television quoted Li as telling the visiting WTO chief, who arrived in Beijing on Sunday after a tour of China's booming economic hub, Shanghai.
China was determined to proceed with negotiations on its entry application to the world trade body, Li said.
Speaking after his meeting with Li, Ruggiero said his talks left him convinced China was determined to take the difficult steps and show the flexibility needed to become a WTO member.
"I detected a clear will to become a member and to be flexible," Ruggiero said in an interview.
He said he had stressed repeatedly in meetings with Li and other senior Chinese officials the need for a sense of urgency and to build on progress achieved in talks last March.
"I came with the right message at the right time," Ruggiero said.

"China must show its own flexibility and make a really credible proposal," he said, adding that he was hoping for breakthroughs on non-discrimination, or creation of a level playing field, as well as market access when talks on China's entry resume in Geneva in May.
Ruggiero said China wanted to see flexibility from its negotiating partners.
China's entry depends on hammering out disputes in bilateral negotiations with other countries, as well as through talks en bloc with WTO members.
Li said China's entry to the WTO, successor organisation to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, should not be politicised, state television said.
"This is unfair," it quoted Li as saying. "The world needs China and China needs the world."

Li also lashed out at inequalities such as sanctions and power politics that he said still marred the world trade system, an apparent veiled reference to the United States, which Beijing regularly accuses of exercising undue international influence.
"This is not in conformity with the principle of equality and mutual benefit and is not in keeping with current world trends," Li said.
Ruggiero on Monday cited the progress achieved in bilateral talks in Geneva last March and urged Beijing to move faster to ensure its admission.

Diplomats from countries involved in China's crucial bilateral talks on WTO entry said they had seen little change in recent weeks in China's position on fundamental issues holding up its application for admission, despite progress in March.
Beijing's next opportunity to lay a new offer on the table will come in late May, when non-discrimination and ensuring an independent body for judicial review will be among the hottest topics.
A wide array of barriers remain to be tackled, diplomats say.

Issues on which bilateral agreement remained distant ranged from opening of China's agriculture markets, financial services, insurance and distribution systems to clarifying controversial subsidies to state industry, they said.
